<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

     arXiv's own render as they are (the logo on the bar, the funder logos on their white
     chips). Important: ar5iv's dark rules are unlayered, as specific as

  /* Wide (the theme's 1280px): the theme lays the body out as a grid whose full-width top rows
     were the band's and its sticky reader bar's. The band takes the first and scrolls away; the
     header, the paper's bar (no site navigation, the paper's controls), takes the second and
     stays in view, the one sticky bar, with the anchor clearance that requires (DESIGN-POLICIES).
     The controls show their names. */
  @media (min-width: 1280px) {
    html { scroll-padding-top: 80px; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome { display: contents; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome > #ds-announcement { grid-area: announce; }

    .arxiv-html-site-chrome .tool-icon { display: none; }
  }
  /* Narrow: the header scrolls away, and the controls show icons (names kept for screen
     readers; Why HTML? goes). The theme's contents panel is fixed below where its old sticky
     bar was, and hidden only once the reader has closed it, so until then it is an invisible box
     over the header and the paper: it shows only while open, under the chrome, in its place in
     the page. The paper's footer (build logs, reporting instructions) keeps the text's side
     inset; the theme gives it none, so it met the screen edges. */
  @media (max-width: 1279px) {

    .arxiv-html-site-chrome .tool-label { position: absolute; width: 1px; height: 1px; overflow: hidden; clip: rect(0 0 0 0); white-space: nowrap; }

<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document"><span id="id1" class="ltx_text" style="position:relative; bottom:-3.0pt;"><img src="2602.02419v2/pics/safeground.png" id="g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:23/21;" width="23" height="21" alt="[Uncaptioned image]"></span> SafeGround: Know When to Trust GUI Grounding Models 
<br class="ltx_break">via Uncertainty Calibration</h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">

<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">

</span>

</span></span></span></span></div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Graphical User Interface (GUI) grounding aims to translate natural language instructions into executable screen coordinates, enabling automated GUI interaction. Nevertheless, incorrect grounding can result in costly, hard-to-reverse actions (e.g., erroneous payment approvals), raising concerns about model reliability.
In this paper, we introduce <span id="abstract1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">SafeGround</span>, an uncertainty-aware framework for GUI grounding models that enables risk-aware predictions through calibrations before testing.
<span id="abstract1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">SafeGround</span> leverages a distribution-aware uncertainty quantification method to capture the spatial dispersion of stochastic samples from outputs of any given model. Then, through the calibration process, <span id="abstract1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">SafeGround</span> derives a test-time decision threshold with statistically guaranteed false discovery rate (FDR) control.
We apply <span id="abstract1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">SafeGround</span> on multiple GUI grounding models for the challenging ScreenSpot-Pro benchmark.
Experimental results show that our uncertainty measure consistently outperforms existing baselines in distinguishing correct from incorrect predictions, while the calibrated threshold reliably enables rigorous risk control and potentials of substantial system-level accuracy improvements.
Across multiple GUI grounding models, <span id="abstract1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">SafeGround</span> improves system-level accuracy by up to 5.38% percentage points over Gemini-only inference.</p>
  
</div><span id="id2" class="ltx_note ltx_role_affiliationnotice"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">†</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">†</sup><span class="ltx_note_type">affiliationnotice: </span>Equal contribution</span></span></span>
<figure id="S0.F1" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.02419v2/icml2026fig1.png" id="S0.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/346;" width="476" height="346" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S0.F1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 1</span>: </span><span id="S0.F1.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">
While existing models may commit costly errors on hard-to-undo actions (e.g., checkout), <span id="S0.F1.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">SafeGround</span> detects high uncertainty and defers the decision via cascading. This mechanism explicitly limits the risk of erroneous actions to a user-specified tolerance.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<figure id="S1.F2" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.02419v2/fig22.png" id="S1.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/191;" width="476" height="191" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S1.F2.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 2</span>: </span><span id="S1.F2.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">
Overview of <span id="S1.F2.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">SafeGround</span>.
Given a GUI input, the model performs multiple stochastic grounding samples to estimate predictive uncertainty.
An uncertainty threshold <math id="S1.F2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>τ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau</annotation></semantics></math> is calibrated on a held-out set under a user-specified risk level (i.e, the maximum error rate).
At test time, predictions with uncertainty <math id="S1.F2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\leq\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>≤</mo><mi>τ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\leq\tau</annotation></semantics></math> are executed directly, while high-uncertainty cases are abstained or cascaded.
Low-uncertainty cases exhibit concentrated region scores, low entropy, and low variance, whereas high-uncertainty cases show dispersed predictions and trigger safety-aware deferral.
</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Graphical User Interface (GUI) grounding is a critical component for autonomous GUI agents, enabling vision-language models (VLMs) to translate natural language instructions into executable screen coordinates <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Nguyen et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cheng et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. Recent advances have substantially improved grounding accuracy across diverse GUI environments, making it increasingly feasible to deploy such agents in real-world applications <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Fan et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hong et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.
However, in practical GUI interactions, a single incorrect grounding can trigger costly and hard-to-reverse actions, including erroneous payment approvals or irreversible system configurations <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.
Despite these risks, existing GUI grounding models typically output only point predictions, offering no indication of when a prediction is unreliable or should be deferred <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gawlikowski et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hu et al., 2023</a>)</cite> as shown in Figure <a href="#S0.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ SafeGround: Know When to Trust GUI Grounding Models via Uncertainty Calibration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The aforementioned limitation of existing GUI grounding models motivates the incorporation of uncertainty quantification (UQ) to enable safer decision-making. However, existing UQ techniques are poorly suited for GUI grounding and remain largely underexplored in this setting <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. In particular, prior approaches suffer from several key limitations. (1) Uncertainty derived from model probabilities or logits <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hendrycks and Gimpel, 2017</a>)</cite> assumes access to internal model states, making it infeasible for black-box vision-language models commonly used in GUI agents <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ye et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2025b</a>)</cite>.
(2) Verbalized self-assessment <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kadavath et al., 2022</a>)</cite> relies on strong instruction-following behavior and often fails when models do not explicitly reason about confidence.
(3) Approaches that estimate uncertainty using ground-truth regions, such as <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al. (2025)</a></cite>, require annotation and cannot be applied at inference time.
(4) Existing methods focus on producing uncertainty scores alone, without specifying how predictions should be acted upon at deployment time (e.g., whether to accept, defer, or abstain) despite this decision being critical in high-stakes GUI interactions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Geifman and El-Yaniv, 2017</a>; <a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2025c</a>)</cite>.
Collectively, these limitations expose a clear gap between existing UQ approaches and the practical requirements of GUI grounding, where uncertainty must be reliable under limited model access and without test-time supervision <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lin et al., 2023</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">To address these challenges, we introduce <span id="S1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">SafeGround</span>, an uncertainty-aware framework that enables risk-aware predictions for existing state-of-the-art GUI grounding models, without requiring access to model internals.
Concretely, as shown in Figure <a href="#S1.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ SafeGround: Know When to Trust GUI Grounding Models via Uncertainty Calibration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>, <span id="S1.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">SafeGround</span> first quantifies the predictive uncertainty of grounding outputs from the spatial distribution of multiple stochastic grounding samples from the same model.
Then, given the model outputs with estimated uncertainty, we adopt a Learn Then Test (LTT) calibration paradigm to select a decision threshold that rigorously controls the false discovery rate (FDR) of accepted grounding predictions. This calibration procedure provides finite-sample guarantees: with high probability, the proportion of incorrect predictions among all accepted actions does not exceed a user-specified risk level <math id="S1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>α</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha</annotation></semantics></math>.
At inference time, <span id="S1.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">SafeGround</span> enables a principled selective prediction mechanism. Predictions deemed reliable under the calibrated threshold are executed directly, while high-uncertainty cases are abstained from or deferred to stronger models for further processing.
Furthermore, with the selective prediction, we realized the cascading inference, where even when the primary model’s base accuracy is limited, we can further leverage external resource to aid the prediction, achieving strong system-level accurarcy.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate <span id="S1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">SafeGround</span> on the challenging ScreenSpot-Pro benchmark across multiple state-of-the-art GUI grounding models. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed uncertainty measure consistently outperforms existing baselines in distinguishing correct from incorrect predictions. Especially, <span id="S1.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">SafeGround</span> achieves reliable FDR control in practice and significantly improves overall system accuracy through selective deferral, validating its effectiveness for high-stakes GUI interaction scenarios. Empirically, <span id="S1.p4.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">SafeGround</span> demonstrates clear system-level accuracy gains across different risk levels. For instance, on ScreenSpot-Pro, uncertainty-aware cascading with Holo1.5-7B achieves 58.66% accuracy at risk level 0.34, improving over Gemini-only inference by 5.38% points.
Our contributions can be summarized as follows:</p>
<ul id="S1.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We propose <span id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">SafeGround</span>, the first framework for uncertainty-aware selective GUI grounding with finite-sample risk guarantees via calibration.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We introduce distribution-aware uncertainty quantification that leverage the spatial dispersion and concentration of stochastic grounding predictions.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We demonstrate that <span id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">SafeGround</span> with uncertainty-calibrated selective prediction enables reliable FDR control and improves system-level accuracy in cascading inference on the ScreenSpot-Pro benchmark.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Related Work</h2>

<section id="S2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.1 </span>GUI Grounding</h3>

<div id="S2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">GUI grounding maps natural language instructions to actionable interface elements or click locations in graphical user interfaces <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Nguyen et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Fan et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. Most existing GUI grounding methods formulate the problem as a text-based coordinate prediction task, where models generate point locations conditioned on the input screenshot and instruction <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2024a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qin et al., 2025b</a>)</cite>.
Recently, motivated by how humans interact with digital interfaces, GUI-Actor introduces an attention-based formulation that aggregates spatial evidence into a single grounding decision <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wu et al., 2025a</a>)</cite>. These methods have achieved strong empirical accuracy across diverse GUI environments. However, most existing approaches produce deterministic point predictions and do not explicitly model predictive uncertainty, limiting their ability to assess decision reliability or defer actions under high uncertainty.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.2 </span>Uncertainty Estimation</h3>

<div id="S2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Uncertainty estimation is widely used to support reliable decision making in AI systems by quantifying the confidence of model predictions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. In large language models, uncertainty has also been derived from probabilistic measures, semantic entropy, or verbalized self-reports <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hou et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2024b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xu et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kuhn et al., 2023b</a>)</cite>. In GUI grounding, uncertainty estimation remains largely underexplored. Existing GUI grounding approaches typically rely on probabilistic uncertainty or verbalized uncertainty, both of which have been shown to be systematically miscalibrated, exhibiting a mismatch between predicted confidence and actual grounding accuracy <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. This misalignment motivates uncertainty estimation methods that rely solely on model outputs while providing more reliable signals for downstream decision-making, as considered in our work.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.3 </span>Learn then Test Calibration</h3>

<div id="S2.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Learn Then Test (LTT) is a post-hoc calibration paradigm that separates model learning from statistical risk control <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Angelopoulos et al., 2022</a>)</cite>. Given a fixed predictive model, LTT frames decision making as a hypothesis testing problem over a low-dimensional decision space, and uses held-out calibration data to identify parameters that satisfy user-specified risk constraints with finite-sample guarantees. Split conformal prediction (SCP) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Angelopoulos and Bates, 2022</a>)</cite> follows this principle by leveraging data splitting and concentration-based confidence bounds to perform valid risk estimation. Prior work builds on this paradigm to enable reliable decision making in large foundation models <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jung et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2025a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2025c</a>; <a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., </a>)</cite>. Our approach also builds on the LTT paradigm and extends it to GUI grounding through uncertainty-based calibration of spatial action decisions for the first time.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Methodology</h2>

<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Problem Formulation and Notations</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Let the GUI grounding model be a function <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f:\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{T}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒳</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒯</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f:\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{T}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{2}</annotation></semantics></math>, which takes a UI screenshot <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x\in\mathcal{X}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒳</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x\in\mathcal{X}</annotation></semantics></math> and a user instruction <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q\in\mathcal{T}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒯</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q\in\mathcal{T}</annotation></semantics></math> as input.
Given an input pair <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(x,q)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(x,q)</annotation></semantics></math>, the model predicts a coordinate <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{y}=(\hat{u},\hat{v})\in\mathbb{R}^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>u</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>,</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>v</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{y}=(\hat{u},\hat{v})\in\mathbb{R}^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> on the screen.
Although the model produces a single point prediction, the ground truth for a target UI element is typically provided as a spatial region on the screen, denoted by <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B^{*}\subset\mathbb{R}^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>B</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo>⊂</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B^{*}\subset\mathbb{R}^{2}</annotation></semantics></math>.
A predicted coordinate is considered correct if and only if it falls within the ground-truth region, which we conclude as an admission function <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A:\mathbb{R}^{2}\times\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R}^{2})\rightarrow\{0,1\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒫</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A:\mathbb{R}^{2}\times\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R}^{2})\rightarrow\{0,1\}</annotation></semantics></math> with <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1</annotation></semantics></math> indicating a correct prediction:</p>
<table id="S3.Ex1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.Ex1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A\big(\hat{y},B^{*}\big)=\begin{cases}1,&amp;\text{if $\hat{y}\in B^{*}$},\\[4.0pt]
0,&amp;\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">(</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>B</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>{</mo><mtable columnspacing="5pt" displaystyle="true" rowspacing="0pt"><mtr><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo></mrow></mtd><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><mrow><mtext>if </mtext><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>B</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo></mrow></mtd><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mtext>otherwise.</mtext></mtd></mtr></mtable></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A\big(\hat{y},B^{*}\big)=\begin{cases}1,&amp;\text{if $\hat{y}\in B^{*}$},\\[4.0pt]
0,&amp;\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">In current coordinate-based GUI grounding models, predictions are deterministic and are not accompanied by explicit uncertainty or confidence estimates, which leaves the trustworthiness of model outputs largely uncharacterized, and may cause users to place unwarranted trust in incorrect predictions, without any indication of potential failure.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>Method Overview</h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To address this issue, we propose <span id="S3.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">SafeGround</span>, an uncertainty-aware GUI grounding framework that can be integrated with diverse state-of-the-art GUI grounding models without requiring access to internal model states, as illustrated in Figure <a href="#S1.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ SafeGround: Know When to Trust GUI Grounding Models via Uncertainty Calibration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>. <span id="S3.SS2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">SafeGround</span> introduce a user-specified risk level <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha\in(0,1)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha\in(0,1)</annotation></semantics></math> that quantifies the maximum tolerable proportion of incorrect predictions, serving as a high-level control signal for how conservatively the system should behave. The risk level <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>α</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha</annotation></semantics></math> is then translated into an uncertainty threshold <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>τ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau</annotation></semantics></math> through a calibration procedure. Specifically, the GUI grounding model’s predictive uncertainty, <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U\!\left(\hat{y}^{(\mathrm{MLG})}\right)\in\mathbb{R}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mpadded style="width:0.622em;" width="0.622em"><mi>U</mi></mpadded><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msup><mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>MLG</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>∈</mo><mi>ℝ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U\!\left(\hat{y}^{(\mathrm{MLG})}\right)\in\mathbb{R}</annotation></semantics></math> for a prediction <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{y}^{(\mathrm{MLG})}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>MLG</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{y}^{(\mathrm{MLG})}</annotation></semantics></math>, is estimated by <span id="S3.SS2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">SafeGround</span> through sampling multiple additional predictions from the GUI grounding model given the same input. The larger values of such uncertainty score indicate lower reliability.
A prediction <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{y}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{y}</annotation></semantics></math> is correct if <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U(\hat{y})\leq\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>U</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mi>τ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U(\hat{y})\leq\tau</annotation></semantics></math> and rejected otherwise, in which case it is deferred to a stronger model. The threshold <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>τ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau</annotation></semantics></math> is chosen such that, among all admitted predictions, the fraction of incorrect ones, measured by the admission function <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A(\hat{y},B^{*})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>B</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A(\hat{y},B^{*})</annotation></semantics></math>, is controlled below <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>α</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.3 </span>Uncertainty Quantification</h3>

<div id="S3.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We first quantify model uncertainty by analyzing the distributional properties of the ranked region scores. Then, three complementary uncertainty measures are introduced, where they are designed to capture complementary failure modes of GUI grounding: local ambiguity among competing targets, global dispersion of belief across regions, and lack of dominant spatial concentration.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Sampling-Based Spatial Distribution Construction</h4>

<div id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To move beyond deterministic point predictions and capture the output distribution of GUI grounding models, we employ a Monte Carlo <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gal and Ghahramani, </a>)</cite> sampling strategy followed by spatial aggregation, drawing inspiration from attention-based aggregation mechanisms in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wu et al., 2025a</a>)</cite>.
Specifically, for each input <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(x,q)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(x,q)</annotation></semantics></math>, we perform <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math> stochastic forward passes of the grounding model, generating a set of coordinates
<math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{S}=\{\hat{y}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^{K}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msup><mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>K</mi></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{S}=\{\hat{y}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^{K}</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{y}^{(i)}\in\mathbb{R}^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{y}^{(i)}\in\mathbb{R}^{2}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">These sampled coordinates are then projected onto a discretized screen grid to estimate a normalized local density map <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>P</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P</annotation></semantics></math>, which empirically characterizes the spatial distribution of the model’s predictions using only sampled outputs from the model.
Intuitively, high density in a localized area indicates model consistency and thus low uncertainty.
To establish object-level representations, we aggregate connected high-density patches in <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>P</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P</annotation></semantics></math> into disjoint regions
<math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{R}=\{R_{m}\}_{m=1}^{M}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℛ</mi><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>M</mi></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{R}=\{R_{m}\}_{m=1}^{M}</annotation></semantics></math> through density-based clustering.
Each region <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{m}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{m}</annotation></semantics></math> is scored by its <span id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">average probability density</span>, denoted as <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S_{m}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S_{m}</annotation></semantics></math>, serving as a proxy for the likelihood that the region corresponds to the intended UI element.
Regions are further ranked such that <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S_{(1)}\geq S_{(2)}\geq\dots\geq S_{(M)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub><mo>≥</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub><mo>≥</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">⋯</mi><mo>≥</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>M</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S_{(1)}\geq S_{(2)}\geq\dots\geq S_{(M)}</annotation></semantics></math>.
More implementation details are provided in the Appendix <a href="#A2.SS3" title="B.3 Spatial Region Construction ‣ Appendix B Details of Experimental Settings ‣ SafeGround: Know When to Trust GUI Grounding Models via Uncertainty Calibration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.3</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Uncertainty Measurement 1. Top-Candidate Ambiguity (TA).</h4>

<div id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To measure the distinctiveness of a certain prediction from a GUI grounding model, we compute the margin between the two leading candidates. A vanishing margin indicates that the model is uncertain between multiple plausible targets (e.g., two identical exit buttons), therefore, we propose the uncertanty score measured by top-candidate ambiguity:</p>
<table id="S3.E1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U_{TA}=\begin{cases}1-\frac{S_{(1)}-S_{(2)}}{S_{(1)}+\epsilon},&amp;\text{if }M\geq 2\\
\max(0.1,1-S_{(1)}),&amp;\text{otherwise}\end{cases}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>U</mi><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>A</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>{</mo><mtable columnspacing="5pt" displaystyle="true" rowspacing="0pt"><mtr><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mstyle displaystyle="false"><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mi>ϵ</mi></mrow></mfrac></mstyle></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow></mtd><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><mrow><mtext>if </mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow><mo>≥</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><mrow><mi>max</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0.1</mn><mo>,</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow></mtd><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mtext>otherwise</mtext></mtd></mtr></mtable></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U_{TA}=\begin{cases}1-\frac{S_{(1)}-S_{(2)}}{S_{(1)}+\epsilon},&amp;\text{if }M\geq 2\\
\max(0.1,1-S_{(1)}),&amp;\text{otherwise}\end{cases}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(1)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ϵ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon</annotation></semantics></math> ensures numerical stability. High <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U_{TA}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>U</mi><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>A</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U_{TA}</annotation></semantics></math> signifies localized confusion at the decision boundary.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Uncertainty Measurement 2. Informational Dispersion (IE).</h4>

<div id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We assess global uncertainty using the entropy of the region score distribution. To ensure a valid probabilistic interpretation, we induce a categorical distribution over the <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math> regions:</p>
<table id="S3.E2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{p}_{i}=\frac{S_{(i)}}{\sum_{j=1}^{M}S_{(j)}}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>p</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><msub><mi>S</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub><mrow><msubsup><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>M</mi></msubsup><msub><mi>S</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{p}_{i}=\frac{S_{(i)}}{\sum_{j=1}^{M}S_{(j)}},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(2)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p1.2" class="ltx_p">and then we define the uncertainty score based on information dispersion as the normalized entropy:</p>
<table id="S3.E3" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E3.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="U_{\text{IE}}=-\frac{1}{\log M}\sum_{i=1}^{M}\hat{p}_{i}\log(\hat{p}_{i}+\epsilon)." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>U</mi><mtext>IE</mtext></msub><mo rspace="0em">=</mo><mo lspace="0em">−</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow></mfrac><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>M</mi></munderover><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>p</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>i</mi></msub><mi>log</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>p</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><mi>ϵ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U_{\text{IE}}=-\frac{1}{\log M}\sum_{i=1}^{M}\hat{p}_{i}\log(\hat{p}_{i}+\epsilon).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(3)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p1.3" class="ltx_p">Such measurement captures the dispersion of probability mass across regions; a high <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U_{\text{IE}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>U</mi><mtext>IE</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U_{\text{IE}}</annotation></semantics></math> indicates that the model’s confidence is fragmented, failing to converge on a single consistent hypothesis.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Uncertainty Measurement 3. Concentration Deficit (CD).</h4>

<div id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">While entropy assesses global disorder, we explicitly quantify the lack of focus with another uncertainty score <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U_{CD}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>U</mi><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>D</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U_{CD}</annotation></semantics></math> by examining the quadratic concentration of the distribution:</p>
<table id="S3.E4" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U_{CD}=1-\sum_{i=1}^{M}\hat{p}_{i}^{2}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>U</mi><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>D</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo rspace="0.055em">−</mo><mrow><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>M</mi></munderover><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>p</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>i</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U_{CD}=1-\sum_{i=1}^{M}\hat{p}_{i}^{2}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(4)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px4.p1.2" class="ltx_p">Unlike entropy, <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U_{CD}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>U</mi><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>D</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U_{CD}</annotation></semantics></math> is more sensitive to the dominance of the top candidates. Higher values of <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px4.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U_{CD}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>U</mi><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>D</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U_{CD}</annotation></semantics></math> indicate a highly fragmented distribution, suggesting that the model lacks a clear spatial focus and distributes confidence across multiple interface regions.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px5" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Combined Uncertainty Score.</h4>

<div id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Each uncertainty score captures a distinct aspect of predictive dispersion, and no single measurement is universally dominant across all models and scenarios.
To obtain a unified and deployment-friendly uncertainty signal, we aggregate these three scores into a single one via a fixed weighted combination:</p>
<table id="S3.E5" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U_{COM}(\hat{y})=w_{CD}\cdot U_{CD}+w_{IE}\cdot U_{IE}+w_{TA}\cdot U_{TA}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>U</mi><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>O</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>D</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msub><mi>U</mi><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>D</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mrow><mi>I</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>E</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msub><mi>U</mi><mrow><mi>I</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>E</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>A</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msub><mi>U</mi><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>A</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U_{COM}(\hat{y})=w_{CD}\cdot U_{CD}+w_{IE}\cdot U_{IE}+w_{TA}\cdot U_{TA}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(5)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px5.p1.2" class="ltx_p">We adopt a single set of weights across all models to preserve a plug-and-play interface without model-specific tuning.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.4 </span>Uncertainty Calibration for Selective Prediction</h3>

<div id="S3.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Although the proposed uncertainty measures capture predictive uncertainty, they cannot fully distinguish between correct and incorrect predictions.
To enable user-specified deployment, we further introduce a selective prediction mechanism by calibrating a statistically rigorous decision threshold <math id="S3.SS4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>τ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau</annotation></semantics></math> on the uncertainty score, such that, among all accepted predictions, the proportion of incorrect predictions does not exceed a desired level <math id="S3.SS4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>α</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Following prior SCP-based frameworks, we hold out a calibration set of <math id="S3.SS4.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>N</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N</annotation></semantics></math> data points: <math id="S3.SS4.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}_{cal}=\{(x_{i},q_{i},B_{i}^{*})\}_{i=1}^{N}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>B</mi><mi>i</mi><mo>∗</mo></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>N</mi></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}_{cal}=\{(x_{i},q_{i},B_{i}^{*})\}_{i=1}^{N}</annotation></semantics></math>.
For each calibration input pair <math id="S3.SS4.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(x_{i},q_{i})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(x_{i},q_{i})</annotation></semantics></math>, we produce <math id="S3.SS4.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{y}_{i}^{(MLG)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>i</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>L</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>G</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{y}_{i}^{(MLG)}</annotation></semantics></math> and quantify its uncertainty score <math id="S3.SS4.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u_{i}=U\left(\hat{y}_{i}^{(MLG)}\right)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>U</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>i</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>L</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>G</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u_{i}=U\left(\hat{y}_{i}^{(MLG)}\right)</annotation></semantics></math>.
Given a candidate threshold <math id="S3.SS4.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>τ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau</annotation></semantics></math>, we obtain the number of accepted predictions <math id="S3.SS4.p2.m7" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\sum_{i}^{N}\mathbf{1}\{u_{i}\leq\tau\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mo>∑</mo><mi>i</mi><mi>N</mi></msubsup><mn>𝟏</mn><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>≤</mo><mi>τ</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sum_{i}^{N}\mathbf{1}\{u_{i}\leq\tau\}</annotation></semantics></math>, and the number of incorrect predictions <math id="S3.SS4.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sum_{i}^{N}\mathbf{1}\{u_{i}\leq\tau,A(\hat{y}_{i}^{(MLG)},B_{i}^{*})=0\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mo>∑</mo><mi>i</mi><mi>N</mi></msubsup><mrow><mn>𝟏</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>≤</mo><mi>τ</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>i</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>L</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>G</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>B</mi><mi>i</mi><mo>∗</mo></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sum_{i}^{N}\mathbf{1}\{u_{i}\leq\tau,A(\hat{y}_{i}^{(MLG)},B_{i}^{*})=0\}</annotation></semantics></math>.
We then compute the false discovery rate (FDR) on <math id="S3.SS4.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}_{cal}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}_{cal}</annotation></semantics></math> under threshold <math id="S3.SS4.p2.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>τ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau</annotation></semantics></math>:</p>
<table id="S3.E6" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{FDR}_{cal}(\tau)=\frac{\sum_{i}^{N}\mathbf{1}\{u_{i}\leq\tau,A(\hat{y}_{i}^{(MLG)},B_{i}^{*})=0\}}{\sum_{i}^{N}\mathbf{1}\{u_{i}\leq\tau\}}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>FDR</mi><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>τ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msubsup><mo>∑</mo><mi>i</mi><mi>N</mi></msubsup><mrow><mn>𝟏</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>≤</mo><mi>τ</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>i</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>L</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>G</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>B</mi><mi>i</mi><mo>∗</mo></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mrow><mo>∑</mo><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub><msup><mrow></mrow><mi>N</mi></msup><mn>𝟏</mn><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>u</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>≤</mo><mi>τ</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{FDR}_{cal}(\tau)=\frac{\sum_{i}^{N}\mathbf{1}\{u_{i}\leq\tau,A(\hat{y}_{i}^{(MLG)},B_{i}^{*})=0\}}{\sum_{i}^{N}\mathbf{1}\{u_{i}\leq\tau\}}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(6)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS4.p2.2" class="ltx_p">To provide finite-sample FDR guarantees for the accepted samples at test time, we first introduce an auxiliary lemma.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS4.p3" class="ltx_para"><span id="S3.SS4.p3.1" class="ltx_inline-logical-block ltx_framed ltx_framed_rectangle">
<span id="S3.Thmtheorem1" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_lemma">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="S3.Thmtheorem1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Lemma 3.1</span></span><span id="S3.Thmtheorem1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> </span>(Clopper–Pearson interval <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Clopper and Pearson, 1934</a>)</cite>)<span id="S3.Thmtheorem1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<span id="S3.Thmtheorem1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<span id="S3.Thmtheorem1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.Thmtheorem1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Let <math id="S3.Thmtheorem1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X\sim\mathrm{Bin}(n,p)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mi>Bin</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X\sim\mathrm{Bin}(n,p)</annotation></semantics></math> be the number of successes in <math id="S3.Thmtheorem1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math> i.i.d. Bernoulli trials with success probability <math id="S3.Thmtheorem1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>p</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p</annotation></semantics></math>.
For any <math id="S3.Thmtheorem1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\delta\in(0,1)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>δ</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\delta\in(0,1)</annotation></semantics></math>, define the Clopper-Pearson confidence interval</span></span>
<span id="S3.E7" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<span><span class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<span class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></span>
<span class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\begin{split}\Bigl[p_{L}(X),\,p_{U}(X)\Bigr]\!=\!\Bigl[&amp;\mathrm{Beta}^{-1}\!\left(\tfrac{\delta}{2};\,X,\,n-X+1\right),\\
&amp;\mathrm{Beta}^{-1}\!\left(1-\tfrac{\delta}{2};\,X+1,\,n-X\right)\Bigr]\end{split}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mtable columnspacing="0pt" displaystyle="true" rowspacing="0pt"><mtr><mtd class="ltx_align_right" columnalign="right"><mrow><mo maxsize="1.600em" minsize="1.600em">[</mo><mi>p</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>L</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo rspace="0.507em">,</mo><mi>p</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>U</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mpadded style="width:0.216em;" width="0.216em"><mo maxsize="1.600em" minsize="1.600em">]</mo></mpadded><mpadded style="width:0.716em;" width="0.716em"><mo>=</mo></mpadded><mo maxsize="1.600em" minsize="1.600em">[</mo></mrow></mtd><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>Beta</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mstyle displaystyle="false"><mfrac><mi>δ</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mstyle><mo rspace="0.337em">,</mo><mi>X</mi><mo rspace="0.337em">,</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>X</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd></mtd><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><mpadded style="width:1.994em;" width="1.994em"><mi>Beta</mi></mpadded><msup><mrow></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mstyle displaystyle="false"><mfrac><mi>δ</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mstyle><mo rspace="0.507em">;</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo rspace="0.507em">,</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo><mo maxsize="1.600em" minsize="1.600em">]</mo></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\begin{split}\Bigl[p_{L}(X),\,p_{U}(X)\Bigr]\!=\!\Bigl[&amp;\mathrm{Beta}^{-1}\!\left(\tfrac{\delta}{2};\,X,\,n-X+1\right),\\
&amp;\mathrm{Beta}^{-1}\!\left(1-\tfrac{\delta}{2};\,X+1,\,n-X\right)\Bigr]\end{split},</annotation></semantics></math></span>
<span class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></span>
<span rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(7)</span></span></span></span>
</span>
<span id="S3.Thmtheorem1.p1.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.Thmtheorem1.p1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">where <math id="S3.Thmtheorem1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{Beta}^{-1}(q;a,b)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>Beta</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>q</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{Beta}^{-1}(q;a,b)</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the <math id="S3.Thmtheorem1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>q</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q</annotation></semantics></math>-quantile from a beta distribution with shape parameters <math id="S3.Thmtheorem1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>a</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.Thmtheorem1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>b</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b</annotation></semantics></math>.
Then the interval has (at least) nominal coverage:</span></span>
<span id="S3.E8" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<span><span class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<span class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></span>
<span class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{P}\!\left(p\in[p_{L}(X),p_{U}(X)]\right)\geq 1-\delta." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mpadded style="width:0.441em;" width="0.441em"><mi>ℙ</mi></mpadded><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>L</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>U</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≥</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>δ</mi></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{P}\!\left(p\in[p_{L}(X),p_{U}(X)]\right)\geq 1-\delta.</annotation></semantics></math></span>
<span class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></span>
<span rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(8)</span></span></span></span>
</span>
</span>
</span></span>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS4.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS4.p4.1" class="ltx_p">In our setting, <math id="S3.SS4.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X=\sum_{i}^{N}\mathbf{1}\{u_{i}\leq\tau,A(\hat{y}_{i}^{(MLG)},B_{i}^{*})=0\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo rspace="0.111em">=</mo><mrow><msubsup><mo>∑</mo><mi>i</mi><mi>N</mi></msubsup><mrow><mn>𝟏</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>≤</mo><mi>τ</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>i</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>L</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>G</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>B</mi><mi>i</mi><mo>∗</mo></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X=\sum_{i}^{N}\mathbf{1}\{u_{i}\leq\tau,A(\hat{y}_{i}^{(MLG)},B_{i}^{*})=0\}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS4.p4.m2" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="n=\sum_{i}^{N}\mathbf{1}\{u_{i}\leq\tau\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo rspace="0.111em">=</mo><msubsup><mo>∑</mo><mi>i</mi><mi>N</mi></msubsup><mn>𝟏</mn><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>≤</mo><mi>τ</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n=\sum_{i}^{N}\mathbf{1}\{u_{i}\leq\tau\}</annotation></semantics></math>.
Since we focus on controlling the upper tail of the system FDR <math id="S3.SS4.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R(\tau)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>τ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R(\tau)</annotation></semantics></math> (thereby constraining test-time FDR), based on Lemma <a href="#S3.Thmtheorem1" title="Lemma 3.1 (Clopper–Pearson interval ( , )). ‣ 3.4 Uncertainty Calibration for Selective Prediction ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ SafeGround: Know When to Trust GUI Grounding Models via Uncertainty Calibration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.1</span></a>, we construct a high-probability upper confidence bound, <math id="S3.SS4.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\mathrm{FDR}}_{1-\delta}^{upper}(\tau)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>FDR</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>δ</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>u</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>τ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\mathrm{FDR}}_{1-\delta}^{upper}(\tau)</annotation></semantics></math>, for <math id="S3.SS4.p4.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R(\tau)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>τ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R(\tau)</annotation></semantics></math>, using its empirical estimate from the calibration data:</p>
<table id="S3.E9" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E9.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\begin{split}\hat{\mathrm{FDR}}_{1-\delta}^{upper}(\tau)&amp;=\mathrm{Beta}\!\left(1-\delta;\,X+1,\,n-X\right)\\
&amp;=\sup\{R:\Pr(\mathrm{Bin}(n,R)\leq X)\geq\delta\}\end{split}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mtable columnspacing="0pt" displaystyle="true" rowspacing="0pt"><mtr><mtd class="ltx_align_right" columnalign="right"><mrow><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>FDR</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>δ</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>u</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>τ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mtd><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mrow><mpadded style="width:1.824em;" width="1.824em"><mi>Beta</mi></mpadded><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>δ</mi></mrow><mo rspace="0.337em">,</mo><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo rspace="0.337em">,</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>X</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd></mtd><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo rspace="0.1389em">=</mo><mrow><mo lspace="0.1389em" movablelimits="false" rspace="0em">sup</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>R</mi><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>Pr</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>Bin</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>R</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mi>X</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≥</mo><mi>δ</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\begin{split}\hat{\mathrm{FDR}}_{1-\delta}^{upper}(\tau)&amp;=\mathrm{Beta}\!\left(1-\delta;\,X+1,\,n-X\right)\\
&amp;=\sup\{R:\Pr(\mathrm{Bin}(n,R)\leq X)\geq\delta\}\end{split},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(9)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS4.p4.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS4.p4.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\mathrm{FDR}}_{1-\delta}^{upper}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>FDR</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>δ</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>u</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\mathrm{FDR}}_{1-\delta}^{upper}</annotation></semantics></math> guarantees</p>

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">

<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E10.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Pr\big(R(\tau)\leq\hat{\mathrm{FDR}}_{1-\delta}^{upper}(\tau)\big)\geq 1-\delta." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>Pr</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>τ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mrow><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>FDR</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>δ</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>u</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>τ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≥</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>δ</mi></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Pr\big(R(\tau)\leq\hat{\mathrm{FDR}}_{1-\delta}^{upper}(\tau)\big)\geq 1-\delta.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
